## Wizard’s Tower

### Role in the Campaign

What wilderness would be complete without a lonely stone tower housing a mad wizard and his arcane experiments? What city lacks an imposing tower belonging to a powerful spell-caster, famous for her knowledge of local denizens and phenomena? Since RPGs have been around, it has been natural to associate towers and wizards. These places offer up boundless opportunities for adventure, housing either a patron, a mentor, an advisor, or a foe.

Usually built to ensure security and privacy, the average wizard’s tower (if one could be so bold as to speak of an average wizard) is built of stone and raised via magical means. It is designed to deter unwanted visitors, to prevent prying eyes, and to provide a quiet and structurally sturdy locale for experiments into new and dangerous magics.

Many wizards will build their towers in remote locations, and even those who choose to live in built-up areas will often locate their towers on the outskirts of settlements. As mentioned, wizards tend to value their privacy and security. Some civic minded mages also keep in mind the potential devastation that might be caused by an experiment gone wrong, and therefore keep their abode at a distance from innocent victims.

Wizardly towers tend to be dangerous places to attempt to penetrate. Aside for the

natural danger resident in the homeowner, these locales tend to be protected by a variety of guards and wards of an arcane nature. Rooftop gargoyles may animate, fearsome constructs may patrol the halls, and the building itself may turn against intruders, with shifting walls and magically locked doors. Some towers lack even a conventional entrance, with ingress and egress depending upon the magical ability to translocate.

Depending upon the nature of the campaign, wizards may play a central role in local government. In a magocracy, the local Lord will doubtless be a wizard, ruling the immediate area from his tower. In more mundane forms of government, some wizards may still be recognized as temporal Lords, depending upon their history of service to the crown. If not the local authority themselves, wizards often serve as advisors and defenders of

Depending upon the nature of the campaign, wizards may play a central role in local government. In a magocracy, the local Lord will doubtless be a wizard, ruling the immediate area from his tower. In more mundane forms of government, some wizards may still be recognized as temporal Lords, depending upon their history of service to the crown. If not the local authority themselves, wizards often serve as advisors and defenders of the local nobility. This depends very much on the personality of the wizards, as some prefer to be left alone to pursue their own agendas.

## Variations on the Theme

A particularly paranoid wizard might build a tower that is completely without windows or doors. The entire building might appear to be one seamless piece of stone or metal, defying anyone to gain entrance. Discussions with the locals will reveal that no one has ever seen anyone enter or leave the tower, but the wizard does simply show up in town sometimes… Is there a regular entrance hidden by illusions? Does the tower require some sort of magical entrance key? Or is there simply a hidden entrance somewhere (of somewhen?) else?

Powerful wizards may make their homes in various locations. One possibility for a wizards tower would be a multidimensional building in which each room actually existed in a different dimension; with doorways simply functioning as portals between them. Entering or leaving such a tower could have unexpected consequences as visitors find themselves deposited in unlikely places.

Similarly, a wizard’s tower might well move through time and space. Perhaps the entire tower moves via teleportation either at its master’s whim or in relation to an

external phenomena, like the phase of the moon. If an adventuring party is in need of assistance from a Wizard who lives in such a tower, their first quest might well be to figure out the pattern of movement of the tower and arrange to be in an appropriate location when it arrives!

## Sample: The Peculiar Tower of Petronious Prime

((Text to be read to players))

When bards gather to sing of the great mages, or when epic tales are told of wizards bold and grim, the name of Petronious Prime never comes up. However, should the conversation ever turn to wizards with particularly bizarre personalities, Petronious proud takes his place of honor.

Before you now, rising some five stories tall, lies the peculiar tower of Petronious Prime, an edifice of such renown that even the hardened adventurers among you cannot completely suppress a jolt of excitement. You are about to meet a legend.

((end player text))

## Overview

Petronious Prime is a wizard of some minor fame, less for his impressive contributions to the study of the arcance than for the bizarre magical tower in which he lives. The tower appears normal, if gaudy, from the exterior, but is anything but once visitors arrive within.

Petronious is now approaching 120 years of age and has spent almost his entire life studying what he describes as the magic of chaos. He has striven to harness unpredictable forces and make them predictable. He has delved deep into the mysteries of translocation magic and the links between the location of objects and their inherent magical energy. His life’s work is embodied in his tower, which to him serves as an almost living extension of his will, but for others serves as a sort of randomized series of unconnected places and things.

Famously irritable, Petronious receives few visitors. Gaining entry to his abode will not prove simple, but it can be achieved if visitors can convince his gatekeeper, a minor construct that Petronious joking calls a “chaos golem”, that their petition will be of interest to the mage.

What is the secret to Petronious’ famous tower? The contents of the tower randomly rearrange themselves at unpredictable intervals. This includes any visitors and their

possessions. Petronious appears able to exercise some control over this phenomena, but no one is sure how the transformations occur or how Petronious molds them to his will.

A typical transformation happens without warning. One moment a visitor might be sitting in a comfortable armchair on the third floor, and the next find himself seated on a potato sack in the cellar. The transformations seem to happen without rhyme or reason – room contents do not move together and sometimes pieces of furniture disappear completely, only to reappear at some random time in the future, likely in another room. During these transformations, the rooms themselves seem to move within the tower. One might be in a library, gazing out a ground floor window at one moment, and suddenly find oneself in a kitchen on the fifth floor.

Only Petronious is capable of interacting with the tower in a structured way. Somehow, the tower exercises a sort of prescience, knowing what Petronious wants or needs and ensures that the appropriate items are handy regardless of the apparent contents of the room. Thus, should Pertronious suddenly desire an apple from the pantry, he might open a drawer on a nearby desk, rummage briefly through the assorted papers and implements within, and then withdraw a fresh, juicy apple, still cool from the cellar.

This mysterious link between Petronious and the tower surprises and awes most visitors. When Petronious is ready to sleep, visitors suddenly realize that his bed is in the room. Should he desire to leave the tower, the front door is in the wall in front of him, even if moments before he was on the top floor. The tower reacts to Petronious’ whims as if it were sentient, but it is important to note that at no time will Petronious ever speak of the tower in this way, or act as if it were anything other than a normal house. He does not speak to the building (“Tower, get me some beer”), he merely wants a beer and the tower makes one available.

For anyone other than Petronious, the experience of his tower usually starts out as amusing, but often turns frustrating or even terrifying. Tales tell of one particular visitor, a distant and unpopular relative of Petronious, who spent a month seeking an exit. The wise man always looks to see what is on the opposite side of any door in the tower before passing through.

## Tower Exterior

The tower of Petronious Prime looks to be five stories tall, with an open roof-top garden. The walls are made of slick black stone of a variety unknown to any geologists in the party. The walls appear seamless, giving the appearance that the entire building

is carved from solid rock, and the only clue to its bizarre nature is the way in which windows randomly appear and disappear around the tower.

The front door is a sturdy, magical portal made of the same material as the rest of the tower exterior. It can only be opened from the inside or by the will of Petronious. It swings soundlessly on unseen hinges.

The keeper of the door is Willis, a chaos golem. Chaos golems are magical constructs, and Willis serves to keep the gawking masses from pestering Petronious. Willis appears on the wall of the tower, next to the front door, as a vaguely humanoid face which extrudes from the rock. Willis’ features are different every time he appears but sometimes resemble a caricature of a previous visitor. Willis will speak with visitors and should he be convinced of their bona fides, he will allow the door to open to permit them entry. It is important to note that Willis is no more predictable than anything else in the tower, and exactly what kinds of petitions he will find worthy varies greatly. Some days he may turn away an adventuring party on a noble quest while admitting someone with a less urgent need.

The position of the front door never appears to change – at least from the outside. It is always on the southern wall of the tower and it is surrounded by pleasant flower beds.

## Tower Interior

How does one describe the interior of rooms which may well change at any moment? Visitors to Petronious’ tower can count on few immutable facts, but there are a couple of things which appear to remain constant. Rooms within the tower are all round, approximately sixty feet in diameter, with a spiral stone staircase rising through the center of the room. Most rooms will have 1-3 windows, though the shape, location, and form of those windows may vary.

Doors, windows, and the stairs are perilous things within the tower, and wise visitors learn to stay in one place, rather than wandering through the structure. Anytime someone passes from one room to another or through a doorway, the DM should randomly determine what is on the other side. Even though it is possible to look through a doorway and see the room on the other side, there is no guarantee that what is seen will still be there when the doorway is traversed.

For the purposes of DMs running the tower, there is a flat 10% chance per 15 mins that the contents of the rooms will randomly change. There is also an 80% chance that

the contents of the rooms will change anytime someone goes up or down a flight of stairs, or uses a door.

The transformation takes place instantly and without warning. Interestingly, the phenomenon never results in injury to people in the tower. Furniture never materializes inside living organisms or in mid-air (where it might fall on unsuspecting victims). The contents of the ever changing rooms appear in a neatly arranged fashion, not a random jumble of furnishings.

Rooms appear to change in a completely random fashion, but generally follow relatively logical patterns (i.e. the contents of any given room will be more or less arranged by function so that beds don’t appear at the same time as the contents of the root cellar). There also appears to be an almost infinite combination of furnishings which come and go. It is dangerous to put anything possessions down in this tower, as the table they are placed on could well vanish (with the items on it) and not return to the tower for a very long time. The exception to this is of course the fact mentioned above that Petronious can retrieve any item he desires at will due to his bond with the tower.

It is important to note that due to the random nature of the shifting of the rooms, it is quite possible to become trapped in the tower unless Petronious himself leads you to the front door. Because the contents of the rooms shift whenever the stairs are used, and because the shifts are random, there is no guarantee that going downstairs to the “ground floor” will result in finding the exit. The main door to the tower is just as likely to be found on the third floor as the first, though through another quirk in the magic of the tower exiting the main door always deposits the traveler outside on the ground and never three stories in the air. Thus it is impossible to predict where one might find the way out, or the kitchen, the bedchambers. Indeed, without the active assistance of Petronious, the tower can become something of a house of horrors. Tales tell of some visitors who eventually threw themselves out of windows to escape.

As mentioned, when the rooms transform they tend to do so in such a way that their contents are distributed logically. When a DM determines that the rooms have shifted, he should consult the following tables to determine the general function of the new room and the new location of the room within the tower.

((begin tables)) Room Functions

11 – 15 Bedroom

16 – 20 Storage Area

21 – 25 Roof-top Garden

## Some sample rooms

### Entryway

1. Doorway

The door to Petronious’ tower is surprisingly flimsy. It is neither warded by magic nor by a strong lock. The magical nature of the tower itself (not to mention his own power) is sufficient protection for Petronious. Anyone entering without the prior approval of Willis, the door warden, will find that as soon as they have passed through the doorway, the room will shift and become a dark, dank, dungeon cell without exits, and it will not shift again until Petronious wills it. Petronious usually remembers to check on prisoners regularly, but he is getting old…

1. Trapdoor

In theory, this trapdoor leads down into a root cellar and general storage area. Obviously, given the nature of the tower, it is just as likely to lead to the roof, or the bathroom.

1. Sitting area

A small sitting area appears recently vacated. A warm cup of mulled cider still sits beside an open journal and a dagger, the tip still wet with blood. A quick scan of the journal reveals, however, that the last entry was made over fifty years ago, apparently by a young woman. A careful read of the entire journal will show that it contains nothing of interest beyond the daily musings of a self-conscious young girl. Anyone familiar with the working of the tower will quickly surmise that these items have been randomly thrown together, but newcomers may find the table’s contents quite a puzzle.

1. Storage

Petronious uses the space behind the stairs in the entryway as a temporary storage area. Boxes, bags, chests, and assorted containers are piled haphazardly here. Although the exact configuration of the pile, as well as the contents of the containers, changes with every shift of the room, the area always remains a cluttered storage space.

1. Cupboards

A couple of tall cupboards are here, one containing hooks upon which are hung various coats, cloaks, hoods, and other outdoor wear. The other contains shelves filled with boots, walking sticks, gloves and similar accoutrements.

1. Stairway

A stone, spiral staircase leads upwards from the entryway to the next level of the tower. All staircases in the tower are identical, and with the exception of the entry level

and the roof-top garden, they all lead both up and down. The stairs are smooth, worn stone and are very treacherous if wet. Even when dry, any attempt to run up or down the stairs carries with it a significant chance of slipping and falling.

## Kitchen

1. Firepit

All cooking is done here, over a bed of hot coals. The fireplace has two rotisseries for roasting meat, as well as a small cauldron suspended over one side of the fire. Although no chimney is visible from the outside of the tower, from the inside the fireplace appears to connect to a flue. Where the smoke goes is something of a mystery.

1. Two long tables serve as preparation space. They are generally cluttered with food in various stages of preparation, kitchen implements, spices, and other cooking essentials. Although the tables always contain at least one (and usually several) completed dishes, suitable for a simple meal, at no time does Petronious actually cook. The food seems to appear from out of nowhere, every time the room shifts. It is always warm, tasty, and fresh.

1. Well

Despite the fact that the kitchen moves between floors like all the other rooms, it contains a small well. Although there is no logical explanation for its presence, the well always produces cold, fresh water. Anyone diving into the well will find that it is approximately 30 feet deep, and the bottom is littered with coins in various denominations, adding up to approximately $100.

1. Kitchen cupboards

These are standard cupboards containing the necessary utensils and flatware of a kitchen. The contents vary depending upon the shifting of the room with the simple pottery being replaced with fine china or silver place settings. Currently, the dishes in the cupboards are of very fine quality, with a set of crystal goblets bearing the crest of a long extinct noble family.

1. Storage

It appears that the kitchen has recently been resupplies, as bags of flour and boxes of various foodstuffs have been piled here pending unpacking. Several small kegs of fine brandy are included in the jumble.

## Magical Laboratory

This floor is dedicated to Petronious’ ongoing magical research. As might be expected, much of his work relates to multi-dimensional spaces and teleportation. The lab should contain at least 3 minor and 1 major magic items in a functional condition and a similar number of non-functional prototypes.

Summoning circle

At one time, Petronious’ research focused on the summoning of extra-dimensional beings. This graven circle of protection was a part of those experiments and served him well in numerous summoning rites. Although he no longer dabbles in such matters, the circle remains functional and requires only the appropriate rituals and invocations to be reactivated.

1. Bookcases

Petronious has traveled widely throughout multiverse, and collected obscure tomes and texts related to things magical. At any given time, there are between 50 and 70 books of lore on these shelves. Most are written in obscure, dead languages, often from other dimensions or planes. Careful study, usually with magical assistance to decipher the arcane languages will allow a wizard character to learn one previously unknown spell per month of study.

1. Work Area

These tables are littered with papers, components, tools, and other paraphernalia related to the creation of magical items. Although Petronious rarely crafts items these days, the area is littered with the detritus of his previous work.

A careful search of the work area will turn up 4-40 components of use in spell casting. 10% of these will be rare, exotic, or expensive components such as the congealed blood of a near extinct monster. 30% will be relatively uncommon, such as powdered gemstone, while 60% will be common components.

The tables will also contain at least 1 functional magic wand, 3 scrolls containing arcane spells, and one miscellaneous magical item. The DM should decide the exact nature of these magic items, depending of course upon the magic level of the campaign in question, but the miscellaneous magic item at least should be an exotic object, never before encountered by the adventuring party. It might well be a beneficial but perilous item, or possible a long lost treasure of renown. Keep in mind though that Petronious is not likely to part easily with any of these items.

1. Strange Portal

A 5-foot diameter sphere of blue light, crackling with energy, hovers about a foot off of the ground. Even the most mundane of characters will be able to sense without any effort that the sphere exudes intense magical energy.

Those more attuned to the arcane will be able to sense the chaotic, turbulent flows of magic that surround the sphere. The portal itself is the heart of the tower, responsible for the extra-dimensional transport of the towers contents. A careful study of the portal – something which would require at least ten years of research – would eventually reveal that the portal exists simultaneously in over a hundred different dimensions.

The portal is, however, an extremely dangerous artifact to experiment with, as it is completely uncontrollable. Merely being in the presence of the portal causes items to randomly transport themselves between dimensions, as evidenced by the behaviour of items within the tower. Anything or anyone that actually enters the portal will be instantly transported at random to another dimension. Unfortunately, each item’s destination is determined at random, so a fully equipped adventurer entering the portal will almost certainly arrive naked. Even if one were fortunate enough to travel to the same dimension as one’s equipment though, one will discover that the actual spatial location of arrival in the new dimension is also completely random, so the traveler and his gear could still arrive in widely separated locations. It is also important to note that there is no “other end” of the portal at the destination, making returning to Petronious’ tower virtually impossible.

Needless to say, adventurers are strongly advised against entering the portal. Anyone casting detection magics on the portal will get a sense of strong chaotic magic and a sense of strong foreboding. DMs should advise players that their characters feel very uneasy about the portal, and even the most mundane of characters should sense something “wrong” about the sphere. Given these hints, anyone choosing to enter the sphere deserves their fate!

If asked, Petronious will be unable to explain the origin of the portal. If pressed about his apparently unique relationship with the chaos of the portal, such as its apparent ability to anticipate his desires and reshape items at his whim, he will speculate that the portal itself has a limited sentience. The study of the Chaos Portal in fact makes up the bulk of his life’s work.

# ESSENTIAL PLACES BIBLE MATERIAL

What is needed is a book full of locations with floor plans in varied scale as appropriate to the size of the place/levels or floors depicted, each plan showing fixtures, furniture, doors and windows, etc. With that depiction there needs be s selection of persons, several each proprietor and worker types and their general abilities, and guidelines for the numbers and sorts of other persons likely encountered in the establishment. With that information for commercial places there needs be a list of goods purveyed and/or services offered. Concluding the treatment for a location, a few brief adventure hooks.

About the only prefatory text really needed is an introductory bit, a discussion of how to make the standard floor plans varies so as to make the same sort of place seem different in a different location, and a discussion of the monetary system employed in the work, how to adapt it to a specific game system--for the one to be used will fit in any literary work simply by using specific coin names.

On request Gary Gygax will supply electronic files from his mss. for the information in the works cited hereafter, and more details of the LA game monetary system if needed.

## EQUIPMENT LISTS

### Note on Prices and Selling

The prices listed for goods and materials represent average values. Depending on the location, rarity, or disposition of the seller, actual costs may vary—sometimes rising to double the listed amount or falling to half or less. Such adjustments are entirely at the discretion of the Game Master, reflecting local economy, scarcity, or simple opportunism.

When selling items to a merchant or purveyor, characters can expect to receive anywhere from 20% to 70% of that merchant’s usual selling price. Thus, an item worth 100 in local currency might bring as little as 20 or as much as 70 when sold, depending on market conditions and the negotiator’s skill. As always, supply and demand in the setting dictate the outcome.

Should a character establish their own place of business, prices are naturally theirs to set. Sales and trade in this case should be resolved through the Game Master’s impartial adjudication, balancing opportunity, realism, and narrative flow.

### Antiquities

### The sale of antiquities follows different principles, as such items often carry historical or cultural value beyond their material worth. Antiquities generally fall into three broad classes

**Coins**: In smaller or isolated communities, old coins are usually treated as little more than curiosities—worth about 10% to 20% less than, or at best equal to, current currency. In more sophisticated or urban markets, however, collectors and numismatists may pay a premium. As a rough measure, small quantities of ancient coins might fetch between 200% and 600% (roll one six-sided die) of their metal value. Larger hoards, being less rare, usually earn a lesser increase—typically 120% to 220% (roll two six-sided dice).

**Jewelry**: Apply the same general rules as for coins, though quantity is rarely a factor. Determine the value of any gemstones included and add their full worth to the metal value before applying the multiplier for antiquity. The craftsmanship, age, and provenance of a piece may significantly enhance its price.

**Objects d’Art**: This category includes all manner of valuable artifacts—antique armor, garments, paintings, tapestries, sculpture, and other works of artistry or devotion. The worth of such items depends entirely on the world of your campaign. Use real-world analogues as a guide, adjusting for rarity and the degree of interest in such things among the people and cultures of your setting.

Arbitrary values are acceptable, provided they remain reasonable and do not eclipse the broader balance of the campaign—except in cases where a singular treasure serves as the central reward of a great adventure. Truly priceless items may exist, but as in all tales, _the really big one usually gets away._

A treasure valued at a million in local currency is not implausible, especially if divided among a party of adventurers—but even then, fortune is fickle. Players may sell too cheaply, misjudge a relic’s worth, or fall prey to swindlers and con artists. Such moments often lead to as much storytelling delight as the adventure itself.

Markets may shift, demand may vanish, or fakes may circulate. The Game Master should use these circumstances to enrich the world and remind players that, in trade as in treasure-hunting, luck and cleverness are as valuable as gold.

**_Extraordinary Items:_** Sale of Extraordinary things is also a different matter.

_Memory Tablets:_ These are pretty dear, and something in the neighborhood of a

$10,000 value is not outrageous. In short supply, the cost might be more than twice that.

of course! Guild members will possibly receive a discount.

_Powers and Like Extraordinary Ability Related Knowledge:_ If for example, your campaign assumes that any Power or the like is worth about at least $1,000 per Grade or AEP it costs to use it, then the sale of such thing to a guild will fetch about half price, to an individual whatever that one will pay. Unique ones, though, are worth at least double the price of the “known and standard” ones.

_Extraordinary Items:_ These are not considered as things one is able to purchase. Their sale value to other than an Avatar is basically the sum of the price of a non- Extraordinary item of the same sort, plus from $1,000 to $10,000 for each special feature. Consider protection bonuses and striking plus harm ones at about the middle to top range and multiply per point. A long spear that adds 10 to weapon precision and 6-8 points of harm is thus worth its normal weapon base plus $72,000 to $90,000 more for its addition to success in striking and its harm. A sword surely has the $10,000 per point addition. Use common sense and base it on the way you want your campaign to run. Any supernatural bonus, 25 or more precision bonus, 17 or more harm bonus, _doubles_ the cost for such. If the long spear noted above was +25 weapon precision and added 17-20 harm. The price would be normal weapon base plus $150,000 to $200,000 doubled,

i.e. $300,000 to $400,000.

Repair: Typical items: are at $1 per harm point to be restored or else 40% to 60% original cost of item.

Cloth/Leather Armor, Wood & Leather Shields, and Special Items: $5 per point of harm removed by repair of the item. Double to $10 or quintuple to $25 if the item is expensive and fragile/complicated or very expensive and very fragile/complicated. Base success chance

c. 70% for complex items, and repair cost is paid before success is determined.

Metal Armor: $25 per point of harm removed by repair of the item if chain armor or metal shield. Plate armor repair is double the former cost, $50 per point of harm removed by repair of the item. Base success chance c. 80% , and repair cost is paid before success is determined.

Sharpening (Pantology enabled): $20 for knife or dagger, $50 for axe-like blade, and $100 for sword. This will increase base damage minimum harm score by 6, but each attack thereafter drops the increase by 1 point per hit. Poor tinkers will add 2 points, average ones will add 4, expert ones will add 6 points as noted.

Used Repaired Items: Type according to LM determination. Cost is from 25% to 75% normal new cost, and condition varies from fair (50% standard to excellent (100%/like new).

## PROTECTION AND COMMAND CIRCLE MATERIALS FOR GEOURGY, NECROURGY & SORCERY

It is generally required that a geourge, necromancer, or sorcerer possess both protection and command circle materials in order to perform acts of summoning, calling, commanding, or creating otherworldly forces or entities. These materials are typically first acquired as part of a practitioner’s magical training or initiation, often drawn from specialized guilds, colleges, or private arcane sources. Such items are costly and difficult to obtain, ranging in value from several thousand to tens of thousands in local currency, depending on availability and quality.

The question naturally arises as to how long these materials last before they must be replenished, for even the finest substances wear thin with repeated use.

If one adopts a lenient interpretation, the materials might suffice for as many as twelve complete pairs of circles before exhaustion sets in and a fresh supply must be acquired. The moderate stance allows seven sets of circles to deplete the stock. The strictest view holds that three sets are all that may be formed before the materials are entirely consumed—three times being the charm, as the saying goes.

In all cases, it should be remembered that such organizations and institutions providing these materials rely on more than membership dues to keep their doors open. The expense of resupply may well serve as a reminder that power has its price, and that the path of the summoner is never maintained without cost.

In many fantasy settings, priests, theurges, and other divine practitioners require both propitiation and votive summoning materials to perform sacred rites or channel divine power. These materials represent the tangible means by which a servant of the gods communes with higher powers, honors divine will, or invokes a response through ritual. The precise nature of such items depends heavily on the deity, faith, and cosmology of the campaign world. Each pantheon and tradition defines what is holy, acceptable, or forbidden; thus, the specifics of these materials must be shaped by the Castle Keeper or Game Master to suit the setting’s theology and tone.

### Still, some general principles can be applied across systems and faiths to guide their use in play

Propitiation Materials are offerings made to appease, honor, or seek favor from a deity or spiritual force. They may include incense, sacred oils, blessed candles, libations, or symbolic items of sacrifice. The value and rarity of such materials should scale with the importance of the rite being performed—minor blessings requiring only common materials, while greater invocations or miracles demand rare, costly, or personally significant offerings.

Votive Summoning Materials serve as conduits for summoning or manifesting divine energy—whether to call forth celestial servitors, sanctify a place, or perform acts of theurgy. These may take the form of relics, inscribed seals, blessed symbols, or carefully prepared components aligned with the deity’s domain. The exact items should reflect both the character’s faith and the setting’s cosmology.

When determining the use or cost of these materials, consider three elements: the rite’s magnitude, the sacred context, and the moral or spiritual weight of the act. A simple prayer for healing might consume a pinch of consecrated dust, while a grand invocation to repel a demon lord could require a gemstone etched with runes and anointed in sanctified oil beneath a full moon.

These guidelines are intentionally flexible to suit any system or campaign. The key principle remains constant across worlds: the physical act of devotion—through offering, sacrifice, or ritual focus—links the mortal to the divine, binding faith to tangible expression within the game world.

**Propitiation Materials:** Blessed oil Blessed water

# Source: CnC Docs/Essential Places 10.30.25_headers_export.md


I

Table of Contents for Essential Places Chapter 1 – Introduction

Chapter 2 – Inn of the Orange Stork Chapter 3 – Tavern

Chapter 4 – Guild Smith of Armor and Weapons for War Chapter 5 – General Store

Chapter 6 – Assassins Guild Chapter 7 – Troll Bridge Chapter 8 – Money Changer Chapter 9 – City Barracks Chapter 10 – Manor House Chapter 11 – Jail House Chapter 12 – Trading Post

Chapter 13 – Manor House Chapter 14 – Mage Guild Chapter 15 – Smithy Chapter 16 – Stable Chapter 17 – Apothecary

Chapter 18 – Harbor and Harbor Masters Office Appendix

Like everyone who runs a role-playing game—whether you style yourself an old school Game Master or Storyteller—you must weave a world of complex people and places for your players to explore. From dark alleys to darker dungeons, parties of wide-eyed adventurers will traipse freely from locale to locale, drinking deeply of your creation.

Whether your players want to plumb the depths of their characters’ deep-rooted Oedipal complexes, or just break things, kill people, and take their stuff, they will invariably visit—often repeatedly—many of the same fundamental places. Essential Places, as it were.

Is there a greater archetypical locale in role-playing than the local inn, where the bartender is a grizzled former adventurer and the wenches are both comely and easily charmed? If that innkeeper only had a gold sovereign for every pup of an adventurer who has been through those swinging doors (or even the oft-broken windows)!

While some Castle Keepers are meticulous about detailing every shop, house, temple, inn, or wide spot in the road in their campaigns, the reality is that most of us wing it when it comes to what exactly the general store looks like, or precisely how many horses the local stable can house. Even if you carefully prepare for every contingency, your players will routinely confound you by insisting on heading across town, away from your painstakingly detailed dwarven armorer, because they’ve heard that some obscure blacksmith has a sale on.

**Essential Places** is intended to provide Castle Keepers with a series of detailed locales, urban and rural, populated by interesting characters that can easily be set down in virtually any campaign. This is not a book of exotic places and peoples to be pillaged and burned (though nothing but your skill prevents players from that), but rather an easy reference library to bring life to some of the more regularly traveled places in the game world. The locales are certainly not mundane or dull, but most are common locations that characters will grow familiar with.

This book does not pretend to detail every nook of every location in exacting precision. It would be much longer if it dwelt on every closet on every floor of every building. In most cases, a locale has a floor plan and a detailed write-up of the areas most likely to be visited by players. Thus, the armorer’s showroom and workshop are described in detail, but the loft upstairs where his apprentice sleeps, while mentioned, is not elaborated upon. Similarly, statistics are given for the armorer himself, but not for his wife.

In keeping with the tradition of the **Gygax Archives**, **Essential Places** is largely a generic sourcebook. Where necessary, character statistics or item descriptions are given for Castles & Crusades, the basic material can be easily incorporated into any fantasy role-playing system. In most cases, there is little need for system-specific statistics, since most of the places in the book offer little opportunity for combat (or at least challenging combat) or other mechanics-heavy activities. Should your players insist on wading through the blood of the common folk contained herein, you should assume that, unless otherwise indicated, the characters they meet are simple folk—easily dispatched. Such behavior should have consequences, however, and the authorities tend to frown upon the murder of peaceful citizens.

Each locale in the book begins with a general discussion of the role of such locations in the typical fantasy campaign. While many of these places are reminiscent of real-world medieval locations, this is not intended to be a work of scholarly history, and considerable liberties are taken in transplanting places and items of various fantastic origins. No single book could hope to fully explore the role of these locales in every style or kind of role-playing fantasy world, but in addition to the general discussion on role, each location includes a few variations—suggesting ways in which a particular locale might differ from the norm.

Following these general descriptions, a sample locale is detailed, ready to be transplanted wholesale into a Castle Keeper’s campaign world. Given the generic nature of the work, some details are necessarily left to the imagination of the reader, but these details are rarely integral to the use of the locale. The identity of the exact deity celebrated in the chapel of a noble manor house, for example, is easily customized by the Castle Keeper prior to use.

Again keeping with the standards of the **Gygax Archives**, generic monetary units are used when values are called for. This system allows for easy use of the material in different systems. The symbol “$” is used to denote currency, but should not be understood to mean “dollars” as we understand them today. The symbol represents whatever the base value of the monetary standard is in a Castle Keeper’s campaign world and can be interpreted accordingly.

The costs and values for items indicated herein are intended to be generally consistent with the value of the same items as detailed in Gary Gygax’s _Essential Facts and Things_.

To sum up, this work provides not only the places themselves with descriptions and maps, but a host of characters and opportunities to become immersed in the day-to-day dealings of the people involved—with just a little effort on your part. Small quests or plot hooks are provided if an evening of play not vital to the main campaign is desired, or the material can be easily expanded into the next major adventure.

So, no longer is it just another nameless inn that is stopped by, but **The Inn of the Orange Stork**, with Roscoe “Jolly” Buridge at the counter, ready to serve the weary travelers. Or a fully populated moneychanger’s place of business, where hard-earned coin is exchanged for more portable gems or the local currency.

With continuity comes a deeper sense of reality to your world, and some of these places may become mainstays—giving your players somewhere to return to again and again, enriching the gaming experience. Many of these can be used in the place of any institution called for on the spur of the moment.

We hope you enjoy what we have assembled here, and that it enhances your world—for both you and your players.

### Yggsburgh

Yggsburgh serves as a central example throughout this book, rooted in the traditions of Gygaxian fantasy. Designed for Castle Keepers of all experience levels, **Essential Places** presents detailed locales that balance familiarity with depth. Each location—inn, guild, or market square—carries cultural and mythical texture to fuel narrative momentum. Yggsburgh anchors regional commerce, drawing caravans and hopeful delvers to its stone gates. Beyond its crowded markets, tiered ramparts rise over fog-bound peaks where dwarven mines lie buried in granite, and keeps cling to the ridgelines—each whispering of treasure or conflict, waiting to be stirred.

As a Castle Keeper, you build a world of complex people and places for players to explore. From dim taverns to ruined dungeons, adventuring parties will wander freely, drinking in your creation. Whether your players chase gold, vengeance, or self-discovery, they will return—again and again—to certain fundamental places. Essential places.

Few are more archetypal than the local inn. The barkeep with a rough past, the charming staff, the low voices sharing rumors over ale—these are bedrocks of any fantasy setting. If that innkeeper earned a gold coin for every pup of an adventurer slamming through those doors—or breaking those windows—he’d rival the local lord in coin.

Some Castle Keepers detail every shop, temple, and stable in advance. But often, we improvise. Maybe you prepared the dwarven armorer—stats, history, voice—and your players instead pursue a nameless blacksmith rumored to charge less. In moments like that, a ready resource can make all the difference.

### What This Book Offers

**Essential Places** provides a suite of richly developed locales, urban and rural, each alive with NPCs and narrative potential. This isn’t a catalog of exotic curiosities to be looted and burned—though players may try—but a toolkit for breathing life into the places they’ll frequent. These are familiar but not bland. Designed for repeated visits, each entry offers grounded design paired with enough flavor to spark creativity.

### A Balanced Approach

This book doesn’t attempt to map every corner of every location. It focuses on the areas players actually use—an inn’s common room, a shop’s front counter—while leaving things like the apprentice’s loft or wine cellar to your imagination. The goal is inspiration, not constraint.

### Structure and Content

Each chapter begins with how that location type works in a typical fantasy world, drawing on medieval roots and adjusting tone—grim, whimsical, or grounded—to match your campaign. It ends with a fully usable example: descriptions, floor plans, key NPCs, all prepped for easy integration.

### How Essential Places Support Adventures

Characters in fantasy games venture far—into wilderness, ruins, and dungeons. But the places they return to between those exploits—where they rest, resupply, and gather stories—matter just as much. These hubs of activity ground your world in texture and rhythm.

Don’t treat them as empty pit stops. Let players linger—haggling over iron nails, puzzling through old maps, catching whispers in a noisy square. Use these moments to seed hooks, build relationships, and set long arcs in motion. From the smith with a sharp ear to the innkeeper who sees too much, everyday moments can shift the path of an entire campaign.

### System-Neutral Design

**Essential Places** is system-neutral, shaped in the spirit of the **Gygax Archives**. It avoids mechanics but includes prompts for handling the unexpected—barter, tension, combat—and nudges toward grounded consequences that keep your world reactive and alive.

### Yggsburgh: A Core Setting for Examples

This book draws on the city-state of Yggsburgh—Gary Gygax’s reimagining of Castle Greyhawk—and its outlying district, the Ounce, to illustrate its locations. Yggsburgh is a fortified, medieval-inspired city of around twenty-two thousand, built on trade and craft. Paved streets and working sewers mark its wealthier quarters, while magic weaves through its shrines, workshops, and the bordering Wynchwood Forest where strange creatures still roam.

For full detail on the city and its region, see _Castle Zagyg: Galleries of the Arch Mage_ by Troll Lord Games, the first volume of a two-part project reviving Gygax’s legendary mega-dungeon.

# CHAPTER 1: COMMUNITIES

Communities of all sorts frequently serve as the traditional starting and ending points for adventures, and innumerable parties of characters have met and disbanded in the taverns and marketplaces of isolated villages, fortified frontier towns, and teeming metropolises. Such places can also serve as venues for quests of all sorts, especially those involving non-hack-and-slay elements like investigation, diplomacy, and trade. Even campaigns encompassing long overland travels or voyages at sea will likely involve occasional stops at settlements or ports to obtain supplies and services beyond what characters in a party can carry or provide for themselves.

Indeed, one of the things that distinguishes a campaign from an unrelated series of dungeon crawls can be the downtime between adventures. Many parties will return again and again to a well-established base of operations, a place where the adventurers can heal up, resupply, and train. Providing a detailed community in which to perform these tasks establishes a sense of continuity, provides a stronger rationale for player characters’ progression in competence and ability, and helps tie together adventures into a cohesive whole.

Unfortunately, game-world versions of such places are often not as unique or interesting as they should be. The intent of this chapter is to provide Game Masters with information, resources, and suggestions to help make adventures and encounters in communities of all sorts more plausible, memorable, and exciting for their players.

To a lesser or greater extent, most traditional communities in the game world are made up of people with many similar interests, goals, backgrounds, and concerns (there can, of course, be marked exceptions to this rule, such as in communities in the throes of division and crisis, or those in which there has been historic isolation and oppression of a weaker group).

The smaller a community is, the more this will be true, the greater the chance that the population will also be racially homogenous, and the narrower the likely gap between the poorest and richest members of the community. Because there is a strong link between wealth and political power, smaller communities will also tend to be more egalitarian and democratic in nature. Everyone will likely know each other, at least by name or appearance, privacy will be limited, and anonymity will likely be nonexistent. Members of small communities are also likely to benefit or suffer fairly equally from circumstances affecting the group as a whole.

The larger a community is, the greater the chance that the population will be racially diverse and that there will be a great economic void between the richest and poorest members of society. Power is also likely to be very unequally distributed, typically ranging from a handful of families or individuals with great political influence to a politically disenfranchised underclass, with the majority of the population falling somewhere in between. Most people will tend to mind their own business as much as

possible and value their privacy, and there will be many individuals about whom the population as a whole knows little or nothing. Benefits or detriments to the community will not always be distributed equally. A new marketplace, for example, is likely to benefit the merchant class more than other members of society, and a famine or other disaster is almost always likely to strike the least affluent hardest.

A small nation-state might consist of little more than a single major community, probably somewhere in size from a large town to a metropolis, including perhaps a number of surrounding villages or smaller towns, most likely dedicated to agriculture and providing food for the capital. Indeed, such relatively small countries often evolved from single cities historically and, despite their size, could often become quite powerful and influential. Such small states will likely be the norm in ancient, medieval, or fantasy game milieus.

A large nation might consist of dozens of cities, hundreds of towns, and thousands of villages and smaller communities. Such larger countries will likely be divided into a number of major regions, typically with up to two or three cities and a number of smaller communities associated with each. While such states will almost always have a unified foreign policy and some form of central government that oversees national-level affairs, they may also be content to leave the administration of regional or local affairs to individual communities. Rome, for example, had a cohesive foreign and national policy that unified its empire, but its central government did not generally involve itself in local politics or administrative matters. In certain looser forms of government — such as confederations, leagues, and weak feudal states — the overall ruler may hold power only by the cooperation of a number of lords or electors, or the central government body might only convene yearly or at longer intervals or in times of crisis. (For more information about nations and the forms of government prevalent in them, see Gary Gygax’s _Nation Builder_).

Indeed, even dependent communities might operate with a high degree of

autonomy, especially if they have the practical clout or distance from their suzerain to insist upon it, or if such semi-independence is to the advantage of the authorities to which they answer. Most European cities during the latter part of the Middle Ages, for example, fell within the territories of various dukes, counts, or kings, but had charters from their lords granting them certain rights and privileges in exchange for various fees and responsibilities.

Communities value their independence, and their charters are sometimes won through hard negotiation and even bloodshed. Because trade and industrial communities have a capability of generating liquid assets in a way with which country estates cannot compete, however, many ambitious lords willingly grant charters in exchange for the cash flow they can provide. Charters granted in this way sometimes reduce the city government to little more than a fundraising organ for the lords — and one that could be dismissed and replaced if it is not successful.

Regardless of whether a community has a charter to operate autonomously or is simply allowed to administer its own local affairs, community government might be markedly different from that of the greater nation itself (e.g., preserving traditions from the community’s history, experimenting with model forms of government proposed by various philosophers, adhering to variations suited to particular circumstances). Even under the autocratic Roman Empire, for example, municipal government was distinctly republican in nature. Similarly, Medieval cities that received their charters from feudal lords were generally organized as communes, a plutocratic form of government in which merchants, craftsman, and businesspeople held political power, often in relation to their experience or rank within various guilds.

# TYPES OF COMMUNITIES

Most communities can be broadly classified as villages, towns, or cities. There are also various sorts of special-purpose communities that can play a role in the game, such as communes, prisons, plantations, and military bases, and these are all described either in this chapter or elsewhere in this book.

The size of a particular community will play a big role in determining what sorts of essential places are present within it. In general, the larger the community, the more sorts of craftsmen, goods, and services of various sorts it can support.

Size of most communities is also closely linked to their proximity to natural resources or trade routes, so the GM should have some plausible reason for why a particular community has attained the size that it has. Communities with little to offer new residents will remain at their current size, or possibly even shrink if the pickings are scarce — perhaps leaving amenities intended for a much larger population to fall into disuse or to be adapted for different purposes. On the other hand, events like establishment of a new trade route or discovery of a previously unexploited resource might cause a period of expansion. Being based in such a “boom town” can make for many exciting adventure hooks, as well as providing adventurers with a familiar base of operations that could plausibly grow to meet some of the more complex needs of higher-level characters.

## Village and Smaller Communities

Several sorts of communities of up to village size can be found in the campaign world, especially in the largely-unorganized borderlands, marches, and wildernesses that constitute the frontiers of many nations — places rich in opportunities for adventure. Even in a fantasy milieu, provided that it functions much like the real world, the vast majority of communities overall will likely be farming villages.

**Thorps** are the smallest sort of communities, typically with a mere 20 to 80 inhabitants. Any particular thorp is 50% likely to be non-permanent in nature and dedicated to seasonal activities — like hunting, quarrying, logging, or herb gathering —

or to public works projects. If any given thorp is a permanent settlement, it is 30% likely that all the inhabitants will be part of the same family or clan. If not engaged in some such specific activity, inhabitants of thorps are more likely than those of larger communities to earn their livings as hunter-gatherers, beggars, bandits, scavengers, or the like, or even to be raiders, scouts, migrants, or refugees from a neighboring nation. A thorp might have one or several family heads, although such de facto community leaders are unlikely to have any formal titles and typically hold an ill-defined equality of status. It is only 40% likely that any particular permanent thorp will have a name. Structures are usually confined to huts, shanties, tents, and lean-tos.

**Hamlets** are larger than thorps but still smaller than true villages, typically with

as many as 400 residents. It is 30% likely that such a community is only temporary in nature, being occupied either seasonally or until a specific task is finished (e.g., the completion of a canal). If permanent, a hamlet will generally have no firm economic base or organized governance, and its inhabitants will typically earn livings as subsistence farmers, hunter-gatherers, or through various cottage industries. If non- permanent in nature, the residents will likely be laborers involved in a public works project, such as building a castle, temple, or road; people engaged in exploiting some rich resource, such as seasonal harvesting of wild plants, hunting of saleable fur or meat animals, prospecting for precious metals or gems, or scavenging from ruins; or even bandits or equivalent lawless groups, including irregular military forces like rebels or unemployed mercenaries. The leading individuals in a hamlet may hold some sort of outside authority — such as bosses of a work group, priests, or rebel officers — although typically no particular post of leadership exists for the hamlet itself, which is more often recognized as a locality than a community. The most substantial structures in such a community are likely to be longhouses or huts, perhaps clustered around the ruin of an older building.

**Villages** are communities of up to 900 inhabitants that have some sort of

government and a specific economic base — which, in most cases, is agriculture, making the majority of people in such places farmers. A typical village might have up to a half-dozen industries, the first two of which will almost always be a blacksmith’s workshop and a mill, the two sorts of industry needed to support day-to-day life in an agricultural community (i.e., a blacksmith to create and repair farm implements and a miller to grind grain for use in bread). The third sort of industry most likely to be present in a village will generally be a small brewery.

Villages do not generally have the resources to construct defenseworks, other than perhaps palisades if some suitable construction material (such as sturdy thorn bushes) and constant threat exists. Many do, however, have some place of refuge — such as a watchtower — to which people can retreat if their community is attacked by raiders. Historically, fortified churches served this purpose from the Dark Ages through the Renaissance, as these structures were generally built with the greatest sense of

permanency in mind and, as a result, tended to be the sturdiest in any particular area. If a village is located in an area where physical threats like monsters or humanoid marauders are present, the able-bodied members of the community will also generally be organized into some sort of militia unit.

**Communes** are religious communities, and might be similar in appearance and many functions to villages, often with the addition of one or more ecclesiastic structures. Most of the members of such a community will be of the same ethos and adhere to the same set of religious beliefs. Reasons for the commune being established as a separate community could include worship of a deity with an agricultural or wilderness orientation; location at some holy site associated with the deity; or, if the members are part of a sect or cult, religious beliefs that differ enough from the norm in the nation in question that its worshippers prefer some measure of isolation.

A typical example of such a community would consist of the rural temple of a high priest, housing for his clergy and other followers, and a cluster of huts, barns, granaries, and storage buildings occupied and run by his peasants (or, alternately homes for craftsmen and a collection of workshops if the commune has a manufacturing rather than an agricultural basis). It is 50% likely, however, that any particular commune consists of laity led by a non-ordained prophet and that its members are part of a religious movement deemed eccentric, heretical, or forbidden by the society at large.

Communes can range in size considerably. The smallest would probably consist of a leader and his extended family or immediate followers, numbering up to about 20 folk, while the largest might have 500 or more members.

**Other sorts of small communities** might also exist in the game world. Non- permanent communities consisting of tents, wagons, or boats might be used by nomadic bands of various sorts and resemble thorps or hamlets in their numbers of inhabitants and organization. Boom towns might spring up in formerly isolated or unsettled areas where a particularly rich resource has been discovered or tract of desirable land has been opened for acquisition. A rush of fortune-seekers may flood in, erecting temporary structures on land that they may or may not own legally. Such places might have organization and facilities comparable to a thorp, hamlet, or even a village, but have a population in the thousands. Such unstable conditions very often breed disease, hardship, exploitation, crime, and violence.

## Towns

Towns are permanent communities of up to several thousand people that typically have a variety of different industries and quite often a diversity of races. Small towns are typically home to as many as 2,000 residents, and large towns to as many as 5,000 inhabitants.

What generally differentiates a town from a village is the presence of a central

market, where people from outlying villages can bring their farm produce or other commodities to sell and trade for the goods and services available in a larger community (unlike villages, towns are also typically not self-sufficient in food). It is 20% likely that a particular town market is noted for the availability or quality of a certain locally produced commodity (e.g., iron ingots, cloth, leather goods, horses).

Towns often have several recognized districts or suburbs. They also generally require a more complex and organized system of governance than a village, and are often run by a body like a citizens’ council headed by a mayor.

Most towns will have a diversity of industries, including those most fundamental ones required by their inhabitants on a daily basis (e.g., greengrocers, bakeries, butcheries, fish-markets, mills, blacksmith shops, breweries). About 30%, however, will also have particular industries they are noted for above and beyond other towns in the same region, and such communities will be magnets both for those who wish to either acquire the fruits of those commercial endeavors or participate in them. Historic examples include towns noted for ceramic wares or armor.

Depending on their layout, resources, and prevailing threats, towns might be entirely walled or may contain a secure area large enough to hold all of the local citizenry — and perhaps even people from outlying communities — for at least short periods of time (e.g., until coastal raiders have dispersed). Such a secure area will often consist of a shell keep or walled precinct at the top of a nearby hill, maintained by the civic government or the town’s feudal ruler.

## Cities

Cities are the largest and most diverse sorts of communities and are considerably more complex in almost every way than smaller communities. Such communities are almost always located along major trade routes, on the banks of navigable rivers, or on the shores of deep water bays, and have ample access to resources like food and fresh water for their populations. In a typical ancient, medieval, or fantasy game milieu, small cities have up to 12,000 inhabitants (one modern definition of a city, in fact, is a settlement of at least 10,000 residents), large cities up to 25,000, and metropolises as many as the economics of the game world can support (e.g., Gary Gygax’s City of Greyhawk had a population of about 40,000, while at its peak imperial Rome itself was home to as many as a million).

Unlike most smaller communities, cities will often be divided into multiple quarters, wards, districts, or precincts — sometimes separated by walls or even with movement between them controlled or interdicted by fortified gates — each with a different purpose and each similar in size to an independent town. These might include craft, trade, mercantile, academic, professional, service, temple, entertainment, underworld, government, residential, and military quarters, each of which might be further subdivided (e.g., market districts might be divided into separate sections for

different types of goods, or residential districts might only allow people of sufficient social standing to live in certain parts of them). Another common pattern is to allot one or more quarters primarily to particular nationalities or races, or to foreigners and visitors generally (both for purposes of providing them with suitable amenities and segregating them from the indigenous population).

Various sections of a city might be set off and identified with distinctive boundary stones marked with specific sorts of symbols or sculptures. Respect for such official markers is generally taken very seriously by the community that has expended the time and effort to erect them. Such markers might also have some sort of reputed or actual relevant magical properties.

Cities are even more likely than towns to have some sort of industry (45% likely) or commodity exchange (30%) that is especially associated with them. The head of government of a city usually has at least the title of Lord Mayor (though often this personage will instead be a high noble of the realm or the ruler of an independent state, holding such titles as Duke, Prince, Doge, or Sultan) and presides over a council of representatives who each have a considerable constituency in the city and without whose organizational skills the administration of such a vast and complex system could not function.

Communities affluent enough to evolve from towns to cities will almost always have the economic resources to create whatever defenseworks they need. Independent cities or those that serve as strategic strongpoints for kingdoms or great nobles will generally be walled, even if they have subsequently fallen on hard times (see Fortifications, below, for more information). Designed to impress as much as to defend, such defenseworks are frequently elaborate and imposing, and sometimes even unique, distinctive, or aesthetically striking. In addition to walls and towers, each gate will likely be defended by a structure equivalent to a keep, and multiple fortifications similar in size to a castle — or even a separate, walled garrison equivalent in size and form to a huge castle — may be incorporated into the defensive line.

Another feature common to cities (and to many towns as well) is the presence of public fountains, which are often erected in prominent areas by civic leaders and organizations, both as public works intended to impress and as practical sites for residents or travelers to obtain water. Edifices of this sort are often reputed to have various magical properties, whether innately as a function of the spring water that flows from them or somehow deliberately imbued through the actions of some being.

Example: **Yggsburgh**. Situated along the converging rivers of the verdant midlands, Yggsburgh is both a thriving city and its encompassing county, unified under a single governing authority. Historically renowned as the seat of learning for the legendary sage Immar, it remains a pilgrimage destination for seekers of arcane and divine knowledge alike. Having survived the upheavals of the great Southern

Rebellion, Yggsburgh has since entered a golden age of trade and scholarship.

## Special-Purpose Communities

Various sorts of special-purpose communities — including military bases, plantations, and prisons (described in Chapter 10: Governmental Places) — can play a role in the game and provide an interesting change of venue from more traditional sites of habitation.

**Military bases** are fortified communities owned and operated by and for standing armies, typically the armed forces of a state (although in a medieval setting other armed groups such as knightly orders or pirate brotherhoods might support equivalent facilities). Such places generally house one or more units of military personnel, store equipment, and facilitate activities like training, equipment testing, and field operations. Military bases can range from small outposts to military cities containing thousands of people. Most are dedicated to supporting a single military or paramilitary organization, such as an army, navy, marine corps, constabulary, militia, watch, or guard force.

Some military bases may belong to nations or states other than those in which they are located, and such facilities are characteristic of imperial powers in particular. Regardless of where they are located, military facilities are often extra-legal jurisdictions not subject to the prevailing civil laws of the land.

Terms applied to particular sorts of military bases generally indicate their sizes or functions. Such terms might include armory, arsenal, barracks, camp, depot, dock, facility, field, fort, fortress, garrison, installation, magazine, post, proving ground, reservation, station, or yard. A strategic defensive line might contain numerous interconnected bases, or effectively constitute a single large military base along its entire length (e.g., 70-mile-long Hadrian’s Wall in northern England).

Whatever they are called or used for, military bases will generally employ stringent security measures, which might include walls, towers, fences, moats, buffer zones (e.g., marches), free-fire zones, and armed patrols. In campaign settings where magic is prolific, spellcasters might even serve as members of military garrisons and apply their abilities to securing military bases or specific areas within them.

Other features of military bases may include facilities like command posts, barracks, armories, arsenals, workshops, supply depots, training areas, dining facilities, and stables. Depending on the purpose of a base or the ethos of its owners, such places might also include chapels, academies, gymnasiums, athletic fields, parks, baths, libraries, hospitals, and amenity vendors (e.g., sutlers). While bases in friendly areas might depend on nearby communities for support, those in frontier areas will likely have adequate stocks of food, water, and other supplies to function indefinitely on their own under hostile conditions or siege.

Not all societies will have military bases, and such special-purpose communities

are likely to be maintained only by nation states that are fairly large, well organized, and have standing military forces. Independent communities like bandit redoubts and some monasteries, however, might essentially conform to the characteristics of military bases.

**Plantations** are large, even huge, farms worked not by individual farmers and their families but by gangs of slaves or hired labor, and were common in many areas in both ancient and Medieval times. Such communities are often largely self-sufficient, having all of the characteristics of a village — including a mill and blacksmith shop — plus quarters for slaves or hired labor, barracks for overseers or troops, and a home for the owner and his family (assuming they reside at the plantation).

Moral orientation of the people running a plantation is usually toward order and often evil (i.e., the very nature of the plantation is to exploit the organized labor of many for the material benefit of just a few). Conditions on a plantation are generally comfortable for the owners, adequate for the overseers, and often terrible for the labor force; providing “luxuries” for workers only cuts into profits unnecessarily. Typically, the labor force of a plantation represents from 50% to 75% of its population, and demographics may be split along these lines, with members of one race or ethnic group running the plantation and the members of another working it.

This sort of community also includes such things as “company towns,” where the sole local industry (e.g., a mine) and all other resources are under the control of a single person or organization.

# BUILDINGS

In a traditional ancient, medieval, Renaissance, or fantasy campaign setting, many of the essential places characters need to visit before, during, and after their adventures will be located in the sorts of structures described here.

In rural areas, villages, and other small communities, many businesses and other essential places will be located in one of two types of buildings: longhouses, and sunken huts or roundhouses. Longhouses are generally rectangular and typically made of plaster-covered wood, with a living space at one end, a workshop in the middle, and an area for livestock or storage at the other. Roundhouses are generally square or round, built on top of a three-foot-deep excavated area, tend to be about 10 to 15 feet across, and consist of a single room that is used as a living area, a workshop, or both.

In towns, cities, and other urban areas, many of the essential places that adventurers need to visit are located in townhouses that are two to five stories in height, and built side-by-side to form long rows that are separated by secondary or main streets. Typically, the ground level of such a structure is used as a workshop and to conduct any necessary sales or business; a basement or back room, if present, might be used for storage or as additional work space. A first floor usually consists of a large dining area toward the front and a kitchen toward the rear of the house. A second floor

is typically devoted to the master’s bed chambers and perhaps rooms for other family members or guests. A third floor is generally used for servant and apprentice living quarters and a fourth floor or attic, if present, is typically used either for storage or extra living space.

Materials used for the construction of townhouses and other urban structures might include stone, brick, or plaster-covered timbers (with perhaps the former, heavier materials being used for the first few stories of a building and the latter, lighter materials being used for the upper stories, interior walls, and floors). Roofing for such buildings might consist of thatch, wood boards or shingles, ceramic tiles, slate tiles, or even lead sheeting, any of which might be sealed with pitch or some similar substance. Doors tend to be simple but sturdy wooden portals with adequate locks and bars on their insides, although main entry doors are often larger and more decorative. What materials are used for a particular building will depend on the use for which it was constructed or adapted, the financial resources of its owner, and local availability of various building resources.

In some quarters of a city, especially industrial or poorer residential districts, smaller, simpler, one-story buildings — perhaps similar to those described as being typical of rural areas and small communities — might be used variously for workshops, businesses, residences, or storage areas.

Likewise, many bigger and more substantial buildings will also be present in urban areas, including large inns and taverns, businesses that require extra space for machinery and equipment (e.g., mills, tanneries, shipyards), and the like. Many such buildings will simply be larger, free-standing versions of the other sorts of buildings described here, up to five-or-so stories in height, and constructed of the same sorts of materials. Others will be voluminous sheds framed in heavy timbers or substantial vaulted or columned halls made of stone.

Many of the essential places characters need to visit will be established in one of the sorts of structures described above. Communities in any particular milieu might also include any number of unique, specialized, or purpose-built craft, trade, mercantile, scholarly, professional, service, religious, entertainment, underworld, or government places.

# PHYSICAL CHARACTERISTICS OF CITIES

In many ways, urban areas are much like dungeons, made up of buildings, alleys, and courtyards rather than walls, doors, rooms, and corridors. Adventures that take place in such areas differ from their dungeon counterparts in a number of major ways, however, including much greater access to resources, restrictions on the use of weapons and spells, and the presence of law-enforcement personnel.

**Access to Resources:** Unlike dungeon and wilderness environments, adventurers can generally buy and sell gear quickly in urban areas. A large city or metropolis

probably has high-level non-player characters and experts in obscure fields of knowledge who can provide assistance and decipher clues. And when player characters are battered and bruised, they can retreat to the comfort of inns, taverns, public baths, and other service places. Freedom to retreat and ready access to marketplaces, workshops of craftsmen and tradesmen, and various characters the party can consult for advice or call upon for assistance also means that the players often have a greater degree of control over the pacing of an urban adventure.

**Weapon and Spell Restrictions:** Laws regarding such things as carrying weapons in public and what sort of restrictions apply to spellcasting vary from community-to-community and include specific restrictions based on their individual experiences, ethos, and concerns. Such laws may not affect all characters equally. A martial artist, for example, is not hampered by a law about peace-bonding weapons, but a priest might be reduced to a fraction of her power — or forced to undignified and illegal efforts to get around local restrictions — if holy symbols of foreign or forbidden gods are confiscated at the city’s gates.

**Law Enforcement:** Another key distinction between adventuring in an urban area and delving into a dungeon is that the latter is, almost by definition, a place where the only law is “kill or be killed.” A community, on the other hand, is held together by a code of laws, many of which are explicitly designed to prevent the sort of behavior that adventurers engage in all the time: killing and looting.

That said, most municipal laws recognize monsters as a threat to the stability the city relies on, and prohibitions about murder rarely apply to monsters such as aberrations or evil outsiders. In some societies, however, evil humanoids — unless they are prohibited from entering a community in the first place — are typically protected by the same laws that protect all the citizens of the city. Being morally degenerate is not generally a crime in and of itself (except in some severely theocratic cities, perhaps, with the magical power to back up the law), and it is evil deeds — or, just as often, chaotic ones — that are against the law. Even when adventurers encounter an evildoer in the act of perpetrating some heinous evil upon the populace of the city, laws tend to frown on the sort of vigilante justice that simply leaves one party dead or otherwise unable to answer for his crimes to the local authorities.

Law is generally enforced in communities by a city guard composed of professional soldiers or policemen (equal to as much as 1% of the population if this also serves as the standing army), a city watch consisting of citizens who have other fulltime occupations (equal to as much as 5% of the population if this also serves as a military reserve force), or both. In conjunction with a standing army — or instead of one, in many cases — such forces may also be responsible for protecting a city from outside attack.

Most of the troops in a guard force will be warriors by profession, with officers of

the same background who generally have specialized or better training or are more

experienced, or members of the local ruling elite who have other occupations appropriate to the community (e.g., priests in a theocracy).

Most of the personnel in a watch force, on the other hand, will be craftsmen, tradesmen, and the like. These part-time soldiers will possibly be led by non- commissioned-officers (i.e., corporals and sergeants) and commissioned officers (e.g., lieutenants and captains) who might be part-timers drawn from the same range of classes as their troops, “player character” types who serve in times of crises, or professional leaders of the same sorts that lead full-time municipal troops.
